headline: New fridge attacks spoil food across Europe

sources.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack (BBC News)
Another cyberattack on supermarket fridges sweeps Europe, leaving food spoiled (CBC News)
Supermarkets across Europe hit by new fridge cyberattacks (NBC News)

chunks.text: On November 2, 2026, a supermarket in Sweden said its fridges and freezers were [[hacked]] and set to 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 Fahrenheit. Overnight, temperatures {{shot up}} in [[cooling units]] at dozens of supermarkets in seven European countries, British media reported. In October, police in France said hackers {{took over}} cooling units at hundreds of stores. Some newly hit units used the same Danish temperature controls targeted in France. Reuters, a news agency, could not confirm the attacks were linked.

verbs.why: Gas prices shoot up during a shortage. Her fever often shoots up at night. Temperatures shot up in cooling units at dozens of supermarkets on November 2, 2026.

verbs.wrong: To watch something from far away
verbs.why: Thieves take over a person's email account and send fake messages. A computer virus takes over a laptop and deletes its files. In October, police in France said hackers took over cooling units at hundreds of stores.

chunks.text: Workers at several Swedish stores {{cleaned out}} freezers and {{threw out}} [[spoiled food]]. Outside one Stockholm store, bags of ruined [[groceries]] {{piled up}}. "Everything is destroyed," a Stockholm supermarket's [[sales manager]] said. In Belgium, the owner of a [[butcher]] chain said the attack {{wiped out}} about 15,000 euros' worth of meat. An Ikea store there was also hit. Ikea could not {{rule out}} problems at other [[locations]].

verbs.correct: To remove everything from a place
verbs.why: We clean out the garage every spring. She cleans out her desk before a new job starts. Workers at several Swedish stores cleaned out their freezers.

verbs.correct: To place something in the trash
verbs.wrong: To sell something at a low price
verbs.why: I throw out old milk after a week. Many bakeries throw out unsold bread at night. Workers at several Swedish stores threw out spoiled food.

verbs.correct: To become a larger and larger amount
verbs.wrong: To lose value over many days
verbs.why: Dirty dishes pile up when I work late. Emails pile up during a long vacation. Outside one Stockholm store, bags of ruined groceries piled up.

verbs.wrong: To count the value of something
verbs.why: A big storm wipes out a farmer's whole crop. One fire wipes out a small family business. A Belgian owner said the attack wiped out about 15,000 euros' worth of meat.

verbs.correct: To say something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To report something to the police
verbs.why: Doctors rule out a serious illness after a few tests. Police rule out an accident after they see the video. Ikea said it could not rule out problems at other locations.

chunks.text: The head of a Belgian fridge company called the problem a [[cyberattack]], an attack on computer systems. He said the units were switched to [[defrost mode]], a setting that makes them warmer. One supermarket group reported only a computer problem. Many store fridges are {{hooked up}} to the internet, so [[technicians]] can repair them from far away. That lets criminals reach them. A [[cybersecurity researcher]] said hackers {{go after}} [[store chains]] because the chains run so many [[control panels]].

verbs.correct: To connect a machine to a network
verbs.wrong: To protect a machine with a code
verbs.why: Technicians hook up the new printer to the office network. The hotel hooks up every TV to the internet. Many store fridges are hooked up to the internet.

verbs.correct: To try to attack a chosen target
verbs.wrong: To give advice to a company
verbs.why: Scammers often go after older people with fake phone calls. Online thieves go after small companies with weak passwords. A researcher said hackers go after store chains because the chains run so many control panels.

chunks.text: No group has {{come forward}} to say it was [[responsible]]. "It is not known who is behind this attack, and it may never be determined," a [[spokesperson]] for Belgium's cybersecurity center said. The researcher said a person who {{logs in}} to an unprotected panel is hard to {{track down}}, because almost no [[traces]] remain. The European Union's top farming official called the attacks "a [[deliberate attempt]]" to [[disrupt]] the way food reaches stores.

verbs.correct: To speak publicly after staying silent
verbs.wrong: To attack again after a delay
verbs.why: Witnesses often come forward after a crime is on the news. A few workers come forward with new facts about their company. No group has come forward to say it was responsible for the attacks.

verbs.correct: To enter a computer system online
verbs.wrong: To make a copy of computer files
verbs.why: I log in to my bank's website every Monday. Students log in to the school system to see their grades. A person who logs in to an unprotected panel leaves almost no traces.

verbs.correct: To find someone after a long search
verbs.wrong: To warn someone about a danger
verbs.why: Reporters track down people who saw the crash. The police track down the driver after a long search. A researcher said a person who logs in to an unprotected panel is hard to track down.

mainIdea.s: Hackers appear to have raised fridge temperatures at supermarkets across Europe in one night, ruining food. No group has said it did this, and an expert says such attackers are hard to find.
mainIdea.why: Temperatures shot up across Europe and stores threw out food. No group has come forward, and a researcher said such hackers are hard to track down.

mainIdea.s: Police have arrested a criminal gang that demanded money from European grocers after a fridge attack. Officials say the gang hacked the fridges because the store owners refused to pay it.
mainIdea.why: Close, but no group has come forward and nobody has been tracked down. It is not known who did it.

mainIdea.s: European food officials told grocery companies to replace old freezers because the machines use too much electricity. Stores will get two years to buy new models, and some expect higher prices.
mainIdea.why: This is about an overnight attack in which temperatures shot up at stores in several countries, not a new rule on electricity.

tf.s: Temperatures shot up in supermarket fridges in several European countries.
tf.why: Cooling units got much hotter overnight at dozens of stores, including stores in Sweden and Belgium.

tf.s: This new wave of attacks hit only stores in France.
tf.why: It hit stores in seven other countries. In October, police in France said hackers took over cooling units at French stores.

tf.s: Stores had to throw out food that the heat had spoiled.
tf.why: Workers cleaned out their freezers, and bags of ruined groceries piled up outside one store in Stockholm.

tf.s: A criminal group came forward and said it was responsible.
tf.why: No group has come forward. A Belgian official said it may never be known who did it.

tf.s: Many store fridges are hooked up to the internet.
tf.why: They are hooked up so technicians can check and repair them from far away, and that also gives criminals a way to reach them.

tf.s: A researcher said these hackers are easy to track down.
tf.why: He said a person who logs in to an unprotected panel is hard to track down, because almost no traces remain.

lines.text: Did you hear what happened at supermarkets in Europe on November 2?
The fridge thing? I thought that was just France, back in October.
So did I. But now it's stores in seven countries. Temperatures {{shot up}} overnight.
Some reached 122 degrees Fahrenheit. It sounds [[like something out of a movie]].
What happened to all the food?
Workers {{cleaned out}} the freezers and {{threw out}} everything. At one store, bags of it {{piled up}} outside.
I hate to see food [[go to waste]].
One owner in Belgium said it {{wiped out}} about 15,000 euros' worth of meat.
How does a hacker even reach a fridge?
Many of them are {{hooked up}} to the internet, so technicians can repair them from far away. That's [[the weak link]].
Nobody knows. No group has {{come forward}}, so it's too early to [[point fingers]].
It's hard. A researcher said someone who {{logs in}} to an open panel leaves almost no traces.
Why would anyone {{go after}} grocery stores?
The big chains run so many panels. An EU official called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply.
Then it's probably only [[a matter of time]] before it happens again.

expressions.def: Used when something useful is not used and is lost

expressions.def: The one part of a system or group most likely to fail
ex: Old passwords are the weak link in our security.

expressions.def: To blame other people for a problem
ex: Let's fix the problem first and not point fingers.

expressions.def: Used to say that something will surely happen, but we do not know when
ex: With this much rain, a flood is only a matter of time.
